strengths: Proposes a practical, low-overhead alternative to RHO-Loss by replacing the auxiliary reference model with an in-context learning approximation, eliminating extra fine-tuning while enabling dynamic re-scoring of examples as the model evolves.

Broad empirical validation across three training paradigms (SFT, DPO, SimPO), four model backbones (LLaMA-3-3B/8B, Qwen-3-4B/8B), and both high-quality and domain-relevant data selection scenarios, with consistent improvements over unweighted training.

Thorough ablations covering the number of in-context holdout demonstrations (k), score-update frequency (R), reweighting vs. percentile filtering, and embedding model choice, which help clarify design sensitivities.
Reports concrete computational overhead measurements (~1.5% vs ~10% for RHO-Loss and ~4% for one-shot), which substantiates the claimed efficiency benefit.
Includes qualitative analyses (response length matching, score distributions across domains, high/low-scoring example inspection) that offer some interpretability of why the method works.
weaknesses: The abstract claims ICA is 'equivalent to a first-order update toward the holdout optimum under a local linearization,' but this equivalence is not actually derived or proven anywhere in the main text or appendix (Appendix A only reproduces the pre-existing RHO-Loss/Mindermann derivation); the paper's own core approximation (Eq. 6, replacing retraining with in-context conditioning) is asserted rather than theoretically justified, so the 'theoretically grounded' framing is somewhat overstated.

Evaluation relies exclusively on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o) computing win rates against target holdout-style outputs, with no human evaluation, no standard alignment benchmarks (e.g., AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, or task-specific metrics), and only one training/evaluation run per configuration (variance is checked in only a single setting and extrapolated to all others).

Baselines are limited to RHO-Loss and One-shot learning; several more recent and directly relevant methods discussed extensively in Related Work (e.g., LESS/Xia et al. 2024, GREATS/Wang et al. 2024, DataRater/Calian et al. 2025, bilevel optimization approaches) are not empirically compared, making it hard to judge the method's competitiveness against the current state of the art.

The evaluation metric (closeness to a target/holdout-like test output) is conceptually very close to the method's own optimization objective (matching holdout distribution), which risks circularity/self-favoring comparisons and may inflate the apparent advantage over standard training.

The key motivating claim that ICL implicitly performs gradient descent (Dai et al. 2023) is a debated, simplified theoretical result (largely shown for restricted/linear-attention settings) that is used here to justify treating in-context conditioning as equivalent to one step of fine-tuning on the holdout set — this leap is not empirically or theoretically validated within the paper.

No experiments testing the method's stated key assumption/limitation — sensitivity to holdout set size, quality, or noise — despite this being flagged as an important caveat in the conclusion; such an ablation would strengthen the paper's practical guidance.

Overhead and scalability analysis is conducted only on a single, relatively small dataset (Yahoo_Answers_Topics, 12k examples) and one small model (3B), leaving open how costs (both ICA scoring and kNN search) scale with larger training sets or longer contexts required for larger holdout sets.

strengths: The paper connects a novel in-context approximation (ICA) to the existing RHO-Loss Bayesian framework for holdout-loss-based data valuation, providing some theoretical grounding for why conditioning on holdout examples in-context can approximate a retrained model's loss.
The method is computationally cheap at inference/training time (~1.5% overhead reported vs. ~10% for RHO-Loss), since it avoids training a separate reference model.

Breadth of empirical coverage: experiments span SFT, DPO, and SimPO objectives, two model families (LLaMA, Qwen) at two scales (3B/4B and 8B), and two data-selection scenarios (high-quality and domain-relevant).
Several reasonable ablations are included (top-k holdout demonstrations, score update frequency R, filtering vs. reweighting, embedding model choice), and a runtime/overhead breakdown is provided.
weaknesses: The central comparison against RHO-Loss—the most relevant and theoretically closest baseline—shows win rates that hover near or below 50% in most settings (e.g., 48.96, 49.92, 50.56, 51.21 in Table 1; 46.85–51.90 in Table 2; 47.20–50.60 in Table 3), i.e., essentially no measurable improvement, which undercuts the paper's central claim that ICA is a superior/competitive alternative to RHO-Loss. The paper frames this as 'comparable performance,' but comparable-to-chance results against the key baseline is a weak basis for the claimed contribution.

The evaluation protocol itself is non-standard and potentially biased: 'win rate' is defined as GPT-4o judging which output is 'closer' to a fixed target/reference response. This is a proxy that may favor superficial stylistic similarity (e.g., length matching as shown in the response-length case study) rather than actual response quality, helpfulness, or alignment with human preferences. No standard benchmarks (e.g., AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, academic task performance) or human evaluation are used to corroborate the GPT-4o judgments.

Each model configuration is trained only once (no repeated training runs), so the reported win rates reflect a single training trajectory; the paper only verifies stability of the (repeated) evaluation step, not training variance, which is the more important source of noise given stochastic optimization of LLM fine-tuning.

The claimed theoretical result in the abstract ('under local linearization, ICA is equivalent to a first-order update toward the holdout optimum') is not actually derived or proven anywhere in the main text or appendix; Appendix A only reproduces the pre-existing Mindermann et al. (2022) RHO-Loss derivation, not a novel analysis of the ICA approximation itself. The core approximation in Eq. 6—that one in-context pass over holdout examples approximates the loss of a model retrained on Dt ∪ Dho—is justified only by an informal appeal to Dai et al. (2023)'s 'ICL as implicit gradient descent' hypothesis, without any direct empirical or theoretical validation of the approximation's fidelity.

The default setting uses R=1 (scores computed once, at initialization, and never updated during training), which contradicts the paper's selling point of 'dynamically reweighting gradient updates as model parameters evolve.' The ablation shows only marginal gains (50.73–52.77% win rate, near chance) from increasing R, suggesting the dynamic re-evaluation component contributes little in practice.

Baseline comparisons are narrow: only RHO-Loss and One-Shot Learning are considered; no comparison to more modern/popular influence-function methods (e.g., LESS, DataInf), gradient-matching, or even simple heuristic filters (perplexity, length, diversity) that are widely used and cited in the related work section.

The experimental setup for 'domain-relevant selection' (holding out one domain from Yahoo Answers or SHP-2 and testing on it) is somewhat artificial and may not reflect realistic deployment scenarios where the 'holdout set' represents a genuinely higher-quality or differently distributed set rather than just a topic split.

Ablation results, while present, are generally weak and near chance level (e.g., k=1 is 43.5%, k=5 is 48%, filtering thresholds all below 50%), making it hard to draw strong conclusions about design choices; many of these differences could plausibly be attributed to noise given only single training runs per configuration.

No analysis of statistical significance (e.g., confidence intervals, multiple seeds) is provided for the main results tables, despite many reported win rates being close to the 50% no-difference threshold.

strengths: Novel and practically useful idea: replacing the reference-model-based holdout loss estimation in RHO-Loss with an in-context approximation (ICA), removing the need for auxiliary fine-tuning while enabling dynamic re-scoring as the model evolves.

Clear theoretical grounding, building explicitly on a reproduced Bayesian derivation from Mindermann et al. (2022) and motivating the ICL approximation via the 'ICL performs implicit fine-tuning' literature.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span SFT, DPO, and SimPO; two model families (LLaMA-3, Qwen-3) at two scales (3B/4B and 8B); both full fine-tuning and LoRA; and two data-selection scenarios (high-quality vs. domain-relevant).

Strong practical efficiency results: the method adds only ~1.5% runtime overhead versus ~10% for RHO-Loss and ~4% for one-shot learning, which is a compelling practical advantage given comparable or better performance.

Reasonably thorough ablations (top-k holdout demonstrations, score update frequency R, filtering vs. reweighting, embedding model choice) that help justify default hyperparameter choices and design decisions (reweighting over hard filtering).
The paper is transparent about limitations, explicitly noting reliance on holdout set quality and the difficulty of extending ICA to on-policy methods like PPO.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o) measuring win rate against target outputs, with no human evaluation and no comparison on standard alignment/instruction-following benchmarks (e.g., AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, Arena-Hard); this makes it hard to assess whether gains reflect genuine downstream quality improvements versus closer surface-level matching to the holdout/test distribution.

Each configuration is trained and evaluated only once (justified by a single repeated-evaluation variance check on one setting), which is a fairly weak basis for claiming statistical robustness of the many reported win-rate differences across 4 models x multiple datasets x 3 training objectives.

Baselines are limited to RHO-Loss and One-Shot learning; no comparison to more recent or stronger data-selection methods mentioned in related work (e.g., LESS/influence functions, Datamodels, GREATS, DataRater), making it unclear how ICA compares to the current state of the art beyond the specific lineage it builds on.

Against RHO-Loss specifically—the most directly comparable and theoretically similar baseline—the method only achieves 'comparable' performance (win rates often near 50%), so the main advantage is efficiency rather than quality, which somewhat tempers the significance of the core contribution.

The holdout and test sets are often constructed via similar domain/quality-score criteria from the same underlying corpus (e.g., SHP-2 Baking top-ranked splits, UltraFeedback quality thresholds), raising a potential concern about distributional closeness between holdout and test sets that could inflate apparent gains from holdout-loss-based selection.

The abstract claims an equivalence between ICA and 'a first-order update toward the holdout optimum' under local linearization, but this derivation does not appear to be clearly presented or proven in the main text, leaving a central theoretical claim under-supported or at least not easy to verify from the manuscript body.

Key hyperparameters (k=3, R=1 as default) are chosen without strong a priori justification, and the ablation sweeps are narrow (e.g., only k in {1,3,5,10} and R in {1,3,5,9} on a single model/dataset combination), limiting generalizability of these findings.

strengths: Presents a conceptually elegant and practical idea: approximating the effect of training on a holdout set via in-context learning rather than requiring an auxiliary reference model (as in RHO-Loss), which meaningfully reduces computational overhead (~1.5% vs ~10% for RHO-Loss).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three alignment paradigms (SFT, DPO, SimPO), multiple model families and scales (LLaMA-3 3B/8B, Qwen-3 4B/8B), and multiple datasets covering both high-quality and domain-relevant selection scenarios.

Thorough ablation studies examining sensitivity to key hyperparameters (top-k holdout examples, score update frequency R, embedding model choice, filtering vs. reweighting), which strengthens the credibility of design choices.

Comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of relevant baselines, including RHO-Loss, One-shot learning, and influence-function-based methods (LESS, GREATS), with attention to fair comparison protocols.

Includes several careful supplementary analyses (excluding holdout from training, training-only-on-holdout ablation, GSM8K noise-robustness experiment, absolute metrics like PPL/BERTScore) that help validate the robustness and non-triviality of the main claims.
Provides a clear theoretical derivation connecting the method to a Bayesian formulation of holdout loss, situating the contribution within an established line of prior work (RHO-Loss).
weaknesses: The primary evaluation metric (GPT-4o judged win rate) relies on a single LLM judge without human validation or inter-rater reliability checks, which is a common but nontrivial limitation for claims of 'better alignment.'

Win rates against RHO-Loss are frequently below 50% across SFT and DPO settings (e.g., 46.73–54.43% in Table 1, 46.85–51.90% in Table 2), indicating the proposed method is often comparable to or slightly worse than RHO-Loss in output quality; the paper's framing of this as 'comparable—and in some cases superior' performance is somewhat generous given the data, and the core contribution is more precisely characterized as an efficiency-quality trade-off rather than a clear performance improvement over the strongest baseline.

The key approximation (Equation 6), that providing holdout examples as in-context demonstrations approximates the effect of actually training on the combined dataset, is motivated only by a loose analogy to Dai et al. (2023) rather than rigorously justified or empirically validated as a good approximation of the true retraining-based holdout loss.

Main experiments use a single training/evaluation run per configuration (with variability analysis relegated to a small appendix study on a single dataset/model pair), limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of reported win rates, especially where margins are close to 50%.

The magnitude of improvement over standard training varies substantially across settings (e.g., 46.73% domain overlap noted in some baselines vs. 93.90% in others) without a clear explanation of what drives this variance, making it harder to predict when the method will be most beneficial.

The method explicitly does not address on-policy settings (e.g., PPO), which is acknowledged but leaves a substantial portion of modern alignment practice (RLHF with online sampling) outside the paper's scope.

Reliance on kNN-based subset selection of holdout examples (for prompt-length feasibility) introduces an additional dependency on embedding model quality, which the ablation shows meaningfully affects results, adding a layer of sensitivity not fully explored (e.g., how selection quality degrades with weaker embeddings or larger holdout sets).

strengths: The paper builds on a reasonably principled Bayesian formulation (extending RHO-Loss/Mindermann et al.) and proposes a computationally lightweight way to approximate the holdout-loss term via in-context learning, avoiding auxiliary reference-model training.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span SFT, DPO, and SimPO across four model backbones (LLaMA-3-3B/8B, Qwen-3-4B/8B) and multiple datasets/domains (high-quality vs. domain-relevant selection scenarios), plus a noisy-CoT GSM8K stress test.

Reasonably thorough ablations on the number of in-context demonstrations (k), score-update frequency (R), reweighting vs. percentile filtering, and embedding choice, which help clarify design sensitivity.

Reported computational overhead (~1.5%) is much lower than RHO-Loss (~10%) and comparable influence-function baselines (LESS/GREATS), which is a practically appealing property if the quality gains hold up.

Some appendix analyses (variability across seeds/evaluations, absolute metrics like PPL/BERTScore, domain-score visualization, qualitative high/low-score examples) add useful supporting evidence beyond the main win-rate tables.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric — GPT-4o-judged win rate for 'closeness to a single target/reference response' — is a questionable proxy for alignment quality, especially for preference-optimization methods (DPO/SimPO) where the goal is not to reproduce a specific reference but to match human preference; this metric may reward stylistic/length mimicry of the holdout set rather than genuine quality improvements (the response-length case study in Appendix D.2 illustrates this concern directly, showing the model learning to be 'short' rather than necessarily 'better').

The key approximation (Eq. 6, replacing retraining on Dt∪Dho with in-context conditioning) is motivated only by a single prior claim (Dai et al., 2023) about ICL mimicking gradient descent, but the paper provides no direct empirical validation that ICA scores actually track true holdout-loss changes (e.g., no correlation analysis between ICA scores and actual post-training holdout loss), leaving the core technical claim largely unverified.

Gains over the strongest and most relevant baselines (LESS, GREATS) are marginal, hovering near 50% win rate in Table 14/Appendix C.3, undermining the paper's main selling point of achieving comparable-or-better quality with much lower overhead — the efficiency argument is well supported, but the quality argument is weak against the more principled influence-function baselines.

Most main experiments use a single training run per configuration (explicitly stated), and while an appendix provides seed/evaluation variability estimates for only one dataset/model pair, this leaves the statistical robustness of the many reported win-rate differences (particularly the narrower ones, e.g., ~2-5 points against RHO-Loss in some settings) largely unsubstantiated.

The holdout set is included directly in the training data for the main experiments (Appendix B.1), which conflates the effect of the reweighting scheme with the effect of simply adding more high-quality data; although Appendix C.5 partially disentangles this, it shows the method's advantage narrows and even reverses relative to RHO-Loss when Dho is excluded from training, suggesting some of the main-table gains are inflated.
Reliance on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o) without any human evaluation or cross-validation with a second judge model raises concerns about judge-specific biases influencing all reported comparisons.

The method's applicability is restricted to off-policy training paradigms; the authors acknowledge but do not address the on-policy (e.g., PPO/RLHF) setting, limiting the scope of the contribution relative to the broader alignment literature.

strengths: Proposes a novel, resource-efficient in-context approximation (ICA) to estimate holdout loss without training a separate reference model, building cleanly on the Bayesian formulation from RHO-Loss.
Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three alignment paradigms (SFT, DPO, SimPO), multiple model families and scales (LLaMA-3-3B/8B, Qwen-3-4B/8B), and both full-parameter and LoRA fine-tuning.
Strong set of baselines including RHO-Loss, One-shot learning, LESS, and GREATS, with fair adoption of each baseline's original selection scheme for comparison.
Thorough ablation studies (top-k holdout examples, score update frequency R, filtering vs. reweighting, embedding model choice) that clarify design choices and their sensitivity.
Reports low computational overhead (~1.5%) relative to baselines (RHO-Loss ~10%, One-shot ~4%), supporting the paper's efficiency claims.

Good supplementary analyses: variance/stability checks across seeds and repeated GPT evaluations, absolute metrics (PPL, BERTScore) corroborating GPT-judged win rates, a noisy-data robustness case study on GSM8K, and qualitative examples illustrating what the ICA score prioritizes.
Clear, well-organized derivation and problem formulation connecting the method to prior theoretical work (Mindermann et al., 2022).
weaknesses: The core approximation (using in-context demonstrations of the holdout set to mimic explicit parameter updates on that set) relies on a contested and only loosely justified claim (citing Dai et al., 2023) rather than a rigorous theoretical bound on the approximation error; no analysis of when/why this approximation may fail beyond a brief discussion of on-policy drift.

Primary evaluation metric (win rate) depends heavily on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o); while PPL/BERTScore are provided as a partial check, these are also somewhat coarse and do not fully substitute for human evaluation or more diverse automatic metrics.

Improvements over the closest and most relevant baseline (RHO-Loss) are often marginal or inconsistent — e.g., win rates against RHO-Loss frequently hover near 50% (46–56%) in Tables 1–3, and in some appendix settings (e.g., excluding holdout data from training, Table 17; GSM8K noisy setting, Table 15) RHO-Loss is competitive with or slightly better than the proposed method — weakening the central efficiency-without-sacrificing-quality claim.

Main results include the holdout set in the training data, which conflates the benefit of the selection/reweighting mechanism with simply having additional high-quality labeled data; the ablation excluding holdout data (Appendix C.5) shows a larger gap to RHO-Loss, suggesting some of the reported gains rely on this design choice.

Experiments use only single training runs for most main results (variance checked only for a subset of settings), and are limited to models up to 8B parameters, leaving open questions about robustness at larger scale.

The method still depends on several additional hyperparameters (k for kNN demonstration selection, R for score update frequency, choice of embedding model) whose optimal values appear dataset/task-dependent, somewhat undermining the claim of being a simple, principled, low-overhead framework.
Explicitly acknowledged but unresolved limitation: the approach does not extend to on-policy methods like PPO, restricting applicability to off-policy alignment settings only.
